In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, a novel approach is taken where the differences are directly represented through the use of a new choice of interpolation function, specifically the logarithmic hyperbolic sine function. This results in the creation of a quasi-interpolation operator that preserves positive values and is linear or convex. It has been demonstrated that the operator's error decreases at a rate proportional to the square of the grid size.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas. By analyzing X-ray and gamma-ray morphologies and spectra, researchers can gain insights into pulsar halo characteristics, including the composition and energy distribution of accelerated particles. Notably, a comparison between observed and simulated pulsar halo distributions offers potential insights into the diffusion barriers encountered by cosmic rays. This article discusses the current understanding of pulsar halos, emphasizing recent findings and the future research opportunities in this field.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using a network of sensors, often provide incomplete and
discrete weather data that can be effectively classified into distinct categories. This paper
introduces an extensive weather classification dataset, analogous to the CIFAR-10 dataset, but with
resized images to accommodate more sensitive weather-sensitive sensors. Evaluations of various
convolutional neural network architectures, including a custom multi-layer design, reveal that
convolutional networks successfully classify weather conditions from images captured by vehicle-mounted
cameras. The proposed approach achieves a accuracy of 81.86%, surpassing other techniques presented
in this study. The dataset and corresponding code will be freely accessible for other researchers.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet controlling them can be challenging due to their complex geometry and nonlinear dynamics. This research presents a novel model-based control approach for soft grippers that uses the Koopman operator theory to capture the dynamics of these soft robots. By leveraging image processing and sensor data, the proposed method can learn and utilize online model updates, streamlining the design and deployment process. This approach is demonstrated in simulations and practical experiments involving a modular soft gripper system, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the minimum energy or maximum output of a complex system, and this challenge is compounded by the numerous variables at play. Classical methods like gradient descent have been successful but flounder when faced with sparsity in the data, leading to poorly informed updates and slow convergence. Our research introduces a novel update rule, the Natural Gradient Descent, which bypasses irrelevant variables and only acts on non-zero components, resulting in significantly faster convergence rates. Our findings also apply to various loss functions and can be generalized to multiple parameters.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide insight into the growth of massive galaxy structures. A relatively young, powerful radio source, J2102+6015, has been discovered at a high redshift of approximately 4.575. This source, which is significantly younger than similar sources found in the past, is thought to be in the initial stages of its growth. Due to its high redshift and young age, J2102+6015 offers valuable opportunities for the study of galaxy evolution and can serve as a reference point for the development of massive black holes at the early stages of their growth.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients using information from both lung cancer CT scans and patient demographics and clinical history. Current clinical survival models are only able to provide generally inaccurate time frames - typically between one to fifteen months - after diagnosis, leaving families and patients unsure about what to expect next. By incorporating data from both CT scans and clinical history, more precise individualized survival predictions can be made. A key challenge for developing such a system is dealing with noisy and irregularly shaped tumor regions during image processing. To address this issue, a method called Joint CT- Clinical Surville Network (JCCSNet) has been proposed, which leverages information from both modalities to create a more accurate representation of lung cancer survival times. The JCCSNet model is composed of two distinct parts: a CT modality component that uses a patch-based convolutional neural network to identify and extract meaningful features from lung cancer images, and a clinical modality component that utilizes a one-way branch convolutional neural network to extract valuable information from patient clinical history. By combining these two components with a Long short-term memory (LSTM) layer, a more accurate lung cancer survival time prediction can be achieved. The JCCSNet model was tested on a dataset of 422 patients and was able to successfully predict their survival times with a high degree of accuracy.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for wavelengths between 10 and 5000 km, with a key outcome being the estimation of matter density amplitude, corresponding to $\Omega_m=0.286_{-0.030-0.017}{_{+0.030+0.017}}$ at $z=3.6$. This technique is a significant advancement, allowing the analysis of primordial non-Gaussianity and enabling the use of quasar spectroscopy as a highly effective tool for investigating the early universe.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. It is shown that a module is 'U(h)-free' if and only if it contains elements generating the module as a module over the subalgebra U(h). Additionally, limits on modules satisfying certain conditions are determined. Specifically, for the Lie algebras G(h), Phi(h) and with parameters a, b, c, certain general modules are classified, and for the Lie algebra with parameters a, b, c, modules satisfying certain conditions regarding generators are described.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in large language models have made it possible to develop open-domain dialogue systems that automatically learn to respond to any input based on their training data. However, existing open-domain dialogue systems face challenges in achieving high performance for users with specific requirements. This study aims to build a role-specific open-domain dialogue system that can adapt to various user roles. To achieve this, it proposes a unified framework that integrates a multi-task learning strategy. This approach allows the dialogue system to simultaneously learn task-agnostic and task-specific abilities, such as understanding user preferences. By leveraging this framework, it is possible to achieve satisfactory performance for users with shared but also unique characteristics. When applied to a dataset containing user roles, the model demonstrates improved performance compared to baseline models.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion and that the SGWMB's power spectrum is directly proportional to the square root of the frequency. They also discovered that the presence of the laser interferometer's angular resolution limit and the incoherence of individual memory signals prevent the SGWMB from exhibiting characteristic patterns at high frequencies. Furthermore, the team estimated that the SGWMB's amplitude will be in the range of $10^{-64}$ - $10^{-61}$ s$^2$ Hz$^{-1}$, and its characteristic frequency will be around $10^{-3}$ Hz. Finally, the scientists speculated that the SGWMB might be detectable with next-generation gravitational wave detectors, specifically with the planned ALENCESTO project, which could potentially detect the SGWMB with an amplitude on the order of $10^{-61}$ s$^2$ Hz$^{-1}$ or rule out such a detection with high confidence.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an elegant explanation for the large mass of neutrinos at the PeV scale through a process known as CP-violating leptogenesis. However, this hypothetical supersymmetry framework is challenged by recent discoveries of cosmic rays containing high-energy neutrinos. We propose a potential solution by incorporating a superwimp dark matter scenario, which suggests that dark matter is primarily composed of neutralinoe, into the leptogenesis framework. However, this scenario requires the neutralino mass to be less than approximately 600 GeV. We suggest that this neutralino mass can be explained by a model where the supersymmetry breaking occurs simultaneously with a phase transition in a metastable state of the universe. This model predicts a significant mass of gravitinoe, which can alter the composition of the cosmic rays containing high-energy neutrinos. Additionally, the proposed model predicts the creation of black holes and gravitational waves during the phase transition, which may have significant implications for various experiments in the future.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design this system, an explicit grammatical structure for messages is assumed, and a network that can transmit data according to this structure is constructed. A noncooperative game theory framework is used to analyze the message transmission process, where players are nodes in the network that can transmit data in predetermined sequences. A neuro-symboling model based on deep generative models is developed to optimize the game and enable each node to strategically transmit data that maximizes its utility while preventing others from benefiting. Demonstrated through simulation results, this proposed system achieves better performance in terms of semantic performance and data transfer rate compared to traditional communication methods.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered considerable interest from researchers due to its diverse applications and the intricate nature of language itself. One critical component of NLP is language modeling, which enables computers to process and generate human language. This study focuses on the vital word prediction in language modeling, with the goal of evaluating different modeling techniques and identifying the most effective approach. A novel hybrid model is proposed, combining Naive Bayes and Latent Semantic Analysis to capture contextual relationships and word meaning, respectively. Experiments were conducted using the Wikipedia dataset, demonstrating that the hybrid model outperforms the Naive Bayes alone in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the results highlights the strengths and limitations of each modeling strategy.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Our proposed framework, a two-stage session-based recommendation method, utilizes Rank Embedding to forecast user preferences in a dataset. The initial stage involves identifying potential items, followed by a second stage that selects the top-ranked items based on a recurrent model's output. By integrating this framework into a Rank Distance Based recommendation system, we notably enhance existing methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance on public datasets. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub.

We examine the behavior of active colloidal dimers, representing pairs of colloids connected by a polymer stalk, as they navigate an activity gradient. We find that these dimers act as optimal organizers, aligning themselves perpendicularly to the gradient and achieving a heightened state of order when the gradient's strength is optimal. This optimal organization is a result of the dimers seeking out the gradient's maximum entropy-producing state through a balance of collective and individual movements. We provide theoretical justification for our experimental observations and offer possible applications for these dimers in controlling active matter.

A thorough approach is outlined for simulating single-phase flow through fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures.

This study centers on the development of techniques to sustain formation flying among a group of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). Maintaining this formation under real-world conditions, where disturbances are present and trajectories diverge, poses a significant challenge. Research has shown that this issue can be addressed through the application of optimal control methods. However, these approaches often rely on linear dynamic models, making them suitable only for minor disturbances. This work presents a more robust solution by incorporating a nonlinear dynamic model through a novel application of the Point Set Registration technique in a large group of UAVs. Furthermore, this method is adapted to detect and respond to potential collisions within a formation of UAVs operating in an indoor environment. To validate this approach, simulations have been conducted using a group of 20 UAVs arranged in various shapes, demonstrating the effectiveness of this strategy under both nominal and complex conditions.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by [Brounton (2020)]. We also introduce a novel lower bound for the Seidel energy.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've found a new type of finite-band potential for the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, which we've linked to a specific type of Jacobi elliptic curve. This new potential offers a way to create a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator with a discrete spectrum, and it also provides insight into the behavior of non-self-adjoint Dirac operators with periodic Schrödinger type.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. The proposed framework accurately models the spatial distribution of RSUs, vehicle relays, and vehicle users with adjustable speeds, and takes into account interference from RSUs and vehicle relays into account. The results indicate that the performance of the network can be significantly improved by utilizing vehicle relays without compromising existing RSU coverage; therefore, this approach offers a promising solution for addressing coverage challenges faced by RSUs in congested areas.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on general knowledge, but its reliability suffers from a significant problem: 0.6% of its articles contain defamatory statements towards individuals. While Wikipedia's notability policy effectively prevents articles from being created about anonymous individuals with minimal credibility, articles about notable individuals with low credibility often slip through. Notably, the English Wikipedia has over 50,000 such biographies, posing a threat to the platform's overall quality. Our research paper presents a machine learning-based approach that uses editing patterns in Wikipedia to automatically label articles about individuals as either notable or low-criteria. We've tested our method using neural networks and demonstrated its efficacy by comparing it to a baseline model using features extracted from text edits and human-made labels. During our evaluation, our model accurately identified articles about individuals with low credibility 93% of the time, accompanied by a false positive rate of 3%.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study presents a novel approach to overcoming this issue by developing a decision-based black-box model that enables zero-shot knowledge distillation without requiring access to the original data or model. Instead, it leverages a set of query samples to train the compact model, which is then able to accurately replicate the original model's behavior. This approach offers greater user anonymity and dependence reduction, while also allowing for the creation of more general and transferable black-box models.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is measured at $(4.3\pm0.5\pm0.3\pm0.6) \times 10^{-4}$, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is measured at $(3.5\pm1.0\pm0.3\pm0.2) \times 10^{-4}$. The $\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ decay mode is found to predominantly occur through an $s\bar{s}$ to $\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ quark transition, and the $\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ decay mode

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of twisted torus bundles, encompassing situations not covered by classical methods. By constructing T-duals from commutative Banach algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$-action, we establish a simple, effective approach. Our results are illustrated through examples, including a case that extends Chen and Mathai's work on T-duality with ${\mathbb R}^3$-action.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we present a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework that circumvents this issue by using peer agents' successful experiences. Our approach leverages multi-agent reinforcement learning to create an innovative method for creating imitation learning datasets without requiring expert input. We have successfully trained a agent to imitate others without the need for such input, and the results show that Co-Imitation Learning significantly outperforms traditional reinforcement learning and imitation learning methods.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results indicate that polarization-adjusted convolutional codes can achieve error-correction performance rivaling that of polar codes with CRC and list decoding, all while requiring less complexity.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses of the hands in the initial frame. We have developed a novel, deep network-based method that excels in real-world applications for its simplicity, high adaptability and robust performance. This method is built around a hand-only representation, allowing for more accurate tracking of hand poses and more reliable object shape reconstruction. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on a large, diverse dataset of synthetic data and a set of challenging real-world scenarios captured using a depth sensor.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in images. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately calculate end-effector pose and predict rotation from a single image. Results show that our method's performance improves with more training data and successfully calculates end-effector pose with an accuracy of around 2cm in a variety of indoor environments.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria for selecting these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks, using the K-neighborhood model as a novel approach.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a neutron star are being conducted, assuming the presence of a mediator particle. Within a framework that incorporates a pseudoscalar mediator, simulations of dark matter particles across various mass ranges are performed, demonstrating that the model produces notably higher neutrino production rates compared to previously reported systems. Notably, the system reveals significant neutrino emission in the surface layers of a neutron star, potentially detectable through earth-based neutrino observatories. Furthermore, the model suggests that neutron star crashes could be a more efficient generator of high-energy neutrinos than any other known astrophysical phenomenon.

The ongoing UNIONS survey, conducting photometric lensing measurements with significant depth over the Canadian Fast Radio Burst local sky, is now being supplemented by new data. To analyze these observations, we employed ShapePipe, a reliable and accurate image processing pipeline that relies on machine learning to handle complex operations and provides robust shape measurements of galaxies. By using ShapePipe, we obtained high-quality results from ShapePipe on the UNIONS/CFIS data, achieving an average ellipticity uncertainty of 0.160 and 0.170 for galaxies with magnitudes of 20 and 23, respectively. To verify the accuracy of our shape measurements, we compared them with existing data and found them to be in good agreement. Furthermore, we used our results to perform a photometric lensing analysis and obtained consistent findings with other methods.

A notable consequence of a finding made by A. Katramatos builds upon previous work by A. Sourav and N. Saradha, extending the classic Kronecker-Weyl theorem. This extension involves the creation of a countable set of vectors, whose rotations in the torus lead to the distribution of points becoming arbitrarily close as the dimension increases. Under certain conditions, the rate at which this closeness occurs is shown to be uniform. Additionally, Katramatos' work has implications for a long-standing problem in diophantine approximation concerning the placement of points in the torus.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-dependent Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its weak exchange, the application of lab-induced magnetic fields has an unusually significant impact on the material's spin structure, causing a reduction in the anisotropy within the crystal structure. Using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance techniques allowed us to detect this anisotropy at spin structure level and track its transition into the next Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase. Data suggests the anisotropy decreases by one order of magnitude for every 1% increase in the applied field, and simulations indicate the material's anisotropy displays field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transitions.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a QCD axion field to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry within various parameter spaces. This study investigates whether a sterile neutrino Acts as a Regeneraton Neutrino, facilitating the formation of dark matter through a quantum gravitational process. To this end, we analyze the influence of an intermediate heavy state within neutrino oscillation and dark matter production scenarios, specifically on the baryon asymmetry. This investigation is conducted within axion-like dark matter frameworks such as the model 'Wishful Thinking'.

This study optimizes the execution time of established upper limits for the stabilizer rank of quantum magic states. The investigation also provides stronger bounds on the quantum error tolerance of classical computing systems due to the connection between stabilizer rank and error tolerance. The analysis is based on unitary equivalence classes of states with limited numerical complexity, leading to the discovery of higher rank states and improved upper limits than previously proposed. Specifically, the research shows that for infinite dimensional systems, the rank of a quantum magic state $|\psi\rangle$ is bounded by $\log\dim|\psi\rangle/\log\alpha+\alpha$, where $\alpha\le 2$. The study also finds that for smaller systems of dimension $d$, the rank of a quantum magic state $|\psi\rangle$ is bounded by $d^{\alpha(d-1)/2}$, and further, the research demonstrates that these improved bounds are substantiated by multiple concrete examples.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, denoted by $\phi$, in a complex quintessence field theory, where the scalar field $\sigma$ is part of a $N$-dimensional complex space. The model includes interactions between $\phi$ and $\sigma$, as well as a potential function $V_{C}(\phi,\sigma)$. However, due to the high dimensionality of the space and the complexity of the fields, any interaction with the fields $\sigma$ is highly suppressed. Consequently, the model can be reduced to a single interacting holographic dark energy model, $(8+3N)[\rho_{\phi p}/2]$, which is equivalent to the standard interacting holographic dark energy model, $(8+3N)\rho_{\phi}$. We assume a perfect fluid and use the FRW metric to derive equations for the state parameter, deceleration parameter, and equation of state parameter, which are in line with observations. Furthermore, we have analyzed the model's stability using the stability conditions and found that the preferred model is the $(8+3N)=8$ model, as it satisfies all stability conditions. We have also estimated the model's parameters within the model's stability range.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four plates for the All-Sky Automated Survey for Variable Stars. This study, which involved 153,892 stars with a high degree of accuracy, gathered essential data on variable stars, including 46,672 stars that exhibited periodic behavior. Researchers identified and characterized 20,317 stars that display different variable patterns, and among these, 18,062 stars have been entered into the VSOLJ database. Specifically, the study focused on RR Lyrae, RR Caccioli, DX, AX, SX Phl, and other types of variable stars. It produced significant outcomes regarding locations in the color-magnitude diagram, periods, and pulsation patterns, which provided insights into space motion, distances, and atmospheric properties. For example, the study provided data on RR Lyrae stars with periods ranging from 0.3 to 1.3 days, and distances based on the Feige 7 zeropoint that range from 18.41 to 19.53 kpc. The entire LAMOST dataset for variable stars is now available online at http://vsgw.lamost.org.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in mobile and embedded devices for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs offer an attractive option for extracting entropy in space-constrained settings. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-TRNG designs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a shortage of redundancy, which hampers their real-world applicability in terms of efficiency and versatility. To address these shortcomings, this paper presents TuRaN, a high-performance SRAM-based TRNG that offers enhanced reliability, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. TuRaN yields superior yield in terms of entropy extraction rate, energy consumption, and latency when compared to prior SRAM-TRNG designs. For example, TuRaN demonstrates an extraction efficiency of 44.1 bits per second, energy expenditure of 1.13 microJoules per 32-bit entropy output, and latency of 0.064 microseconds at a 180nm technology node. Moreover, TuRaN can function seamlessly at 100km/s access speed and features a compact area of 0.0004mm^2.

A theoretical model of a single-electron resistive switch is developed using a dimer molecule, allowing for the calculation of energy barriers and hopping distances via ab-initio simulations. For 1 nm wide electrodes separated by 1.5 nm, the predicted operating voltage is around 0.5V. Various configurations are examined, including different molecule orientations and the presence of solvent molecules, which significantly affect energy barriers and hopping distances. However, even with optimal molecule orientations, the predicted operating voltages exceed 1V due to high energy barriers. Nevertheless, reducing molecule sizes or utilizing smaller energy confining potentials could potentially lower operating voltages.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies and propose possible solutions. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of all-loop causal representation for numerical evaluations of multi-loop Feynman integrals.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. Additionally, this proof leads to a precise formula for the spectral measure, as well as an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two optomechanical cavities, this study $q$-deforms both mechanical and optical modes, examining the resulting optomechanical interactions. Notably, the work uncovers that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows for both bright and dark states. Furthermore, for a specified mechanical frequency, the system can produce nearly complete transmission optical windows for both bright and dark states. This research offers a valuable addition to understanding optomechanical interactions and may provide a useful technical application.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we reveal various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. Our analysis demonstrates that these instabilities are correlated with a "Fick" term in the chemical potential's gradient and identifies the origin of a 30 meV energy gap observed in photoemission spectroscopy as a result of quantum fluctuations.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an alternative distribution, known as the L\'evy distribution, that describes the sum of symmetric, independent, and identically distributed variables with stable distributions. This particular form of diffusion has been observed in disordered systems, yet its existence is relatively underrepresented in comparison to Gaussian diffusion. In this study, researchers presented a theoretical model illustrating the anomalous diffusion exhibited by atoms trapped in an optical lattice, and this phenomenon is caused by laser cooling processes resulting in power-law distributed fluctuations. The resulting behavior aligns with the empirical observations reported by Bayerle et al. in 2015, and this finding also sparks potential applications in the exploration of $\alpha$-stable distributions and L\'evy processes.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. By constructing an asymmetric cryptocurrency trading network, the research examines how price information influences node performance and captures high-order interactions among nodes. The analysis employs a high-performance technique called the outside corner search algorithm (OCSA) to identify the optimal solution for complex systems. The results indicate that leading cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum act as hubs, with their price changes affecting other nodes. However, the study also reveals that certain smaller cryptocurrencies are highly sensitive to Ethereum's price, implying they are closely connected to the Ethereum market. The research further finds that during periods of high volatility, the trading volumes of certain nodes increase, while the structure of the network becomes more complex, given that higher-order interactions among nodes become statistically significant.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at temperature 238K. The results indicate a notable shift in the distribution of sulphuric acid and water in the 1:4 cluster when accounting for zero-point motion, as opposed to its classical counterpart. Furthermore, the findings suggest that zero-point motion has a significant impact on the energy associated with sulphuric acid and water in small clusters, which may also affect the potential energy linked to hydrogen bonding.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, and it's shown that compact perception pairs are unique up to isometry.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model and other examples, they examine the relationships between thermal voltage, heat current, and temperature gradient, and reveal that this thermal analogy fails in several cases where Einstein relations are also violated. Importantly, these results show that thermal Hall conductivity can deviate from the conventional expectation based on the local thermal charge.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures and the role of data augmentation in enhancing their performance.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate decision-making processes and the consequences of different decision-making methods.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to balance transaction verification and anonymity makes it an appealing option for medium to large-scale blockchain applications.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these same data structures can be employed to establish the desired class of solvers in space-computational settings.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  The data also show a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, specifically 15.9 (with a statistical uncertainty of 1.4) femtobarns, with a branching ratio of 0.33 for same-flavor boson production and a same-sign tri-boson mass threshold of 750 GeV.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, which has evolved significantly due to increased exposure in the digital age. To address this issue, a new, open-access Universal Dependencies (UD) Hebrew treebank has been developed. This newly created corpus is based on recent linguistic research and is comprised of texts from various sources, including news articles from Haaretz and educational materials from the Hebrew University's corpus. Composed of 26,000 sentences, this UD Hebrew treebank offers a more accurate and inclusive representation of the language. Building upon the successes of past NLP efforts, this new corpus seeks to stimulate current research in state-of-the-art, transparent, and effective NLP approaches. To this end, a new benchmark for Hebrew dependency parsing has been established, which includes the complete UD annotations as well as a set of cleaned and pre-processed texts for easy access.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $ \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} \leq \varepsilon^p \mu(\sup\{ |x_k| : k \in \{1,\ldots,n\} \})^p + \varepsilon \hat{K}^p$, where $\hat{K} = (2K)^p$, holds, and here $\|x_i - x_j\|_{L_p(\mu)}$ denotes the $L_p(\mu)$ distance between $x_i$ and $x_j$. Furthermore, the vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n$

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, enabling the direct analysis of experimental data without the need for analytical solving. This article discusses the development of cooperative data-driven modeling (CDM), a collective approach that leverages the collaboration of researchers to create robust, universal models of complex physical systems. CDM is illustrated using a simple example and is then applied to a more intricate problem involving a nonlinear partial differential equation. The results demonstrate that CDM can yield accurate and generalizable models, especially when researchers work together to analyze extensive experimental datasets.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially leading to suboptimal outcomes.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures safe system operation with minimal deviations from optimal control, while maintaining algorithmic efficiency. Consequently, the computational burden associated with traditional MPSF designs is significantly reduced. This is particularly evident in multi-objective optimal control strategies involving integral robustness metrics, where the number of constraints grows rapidly. Therefore, the computational time required for MPSF design in such scenarios becomes excessively high, making it practically unusable. In contrast, the SL-MPSF design offers superior scalability and performance without compromise. The proposed method is supported by concrete numerical examples that highlight its computational advantages.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. The successful execution of this attack reveals that simply increasing the random phase of light sources does not sufficiently safeguard the system, highlighting the need for an improved protocol to safeguard against quantum hacking.

Language models of significant size have recently shown the ability to learn within context, a capability previously reserved for task-oriented fine-tuning. We examined this phenomenon using a large language model with over 1.9 billion parameters, and our analysis revealed that it can adapt to new tasks through in-context learning with a dataset of approximately 120 thousand examples. Our investigation into the influence of pretraining corpora revealed that a small fraction of pretraining data (around one percent) has a substantial impact on the model's capacity for in-context learning. Additionally, we discovered that pretraining on data containing out-of-vocabulary words leads to enhanced performance in tasks involving unknown words. Our findings emphasize the importance of diverse pretraining data in unlocking the full potential of in-context learning in large language models.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate this process, we have developed a three-dimensional numerical model that balances thermal conduction, magnetic fields, and radiative cooling to study the emergence and dissolution of cold clouds within the hot intracluster environment. Our simulations reveal that when the hot surrounding gas to the cold cloud ratio exceeds a threshold of approximately 36, the cold material rapidly disperses, whereas below this threshold the cold cloud continues to grow. Interestingly, our results indicate that the rate at which the cold cloud expands is directly proportional to the square of the cluster entropy and the conductivity of the surrounding gas, suggesting a predictable pattern of expansion and loss. Ultimately, our findings have implications for our understanding of the long-term evolution of cold cores and the potential for their continued existence in the future.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. Given
the rapidly expanding data sets from the LHC, this area of research is now more
significant than ever. The presentation outlines recent findings from the
ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments, discussing results that may signal
trends towards $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm hadrons, essential for
further investigation.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists between these amplitudes and a certain symmetric polynomial of tree amplitudes, known as BB-polynomial. This relationship is similar to the one observed in 10D open superstring theory, proposed by Gross in 1988. To extend Gross' conjecture to string theory, a complete proof is provided for bosonic string theory with any central extension, and substantial evidence is offered for the general case without a proof. Additionally, the generalized Gross' conjecture is applied to derive a strict upper bound on a specific type of amplitudes, known as NNamplitudes, which are further investigated under the twisted sector of the spacetime.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize energy consumption and waste minimization when deploying computation-intensive applications, allowing for a greener and more efficient MN. This paper presents self-organizing strategies for sustainable MNs by incorporating autonomic scaling of edge computing and radio access network resources at the base station level. Our approach leverages machine learning and neural network techniques to develop simple procedures that promote energy-efficient edge computing and optimize the processing of application data at the base stations. Our procedures are designed to respond autonomously to changing network conditions, eliminating the need for complex manual management. Simulation results show that these self-organizing procedures lead to significant reductions in energy consumption and bit rate, substantially improving the efficiency of MNs.

This research explores the feasibility of building a speech synthesis system
without linguistic resources by transforming the training data into acoustic units
based on sound patterns rather than letter patterns. We've developed an unsupervised
Acoustic Unit Model and a corresponding graph-based representation of sounds
to create a dataset-independent framework for the task. We've also designed an
unsupervised learning framework as well as a data-driven approach to building a
synthesizer model, all of which are grounded in phonetic units rather than linguistic
units. We evaluate our approach using data from zero-resource languages Toda and Yawo.
We compare the quality of our generated speech to that of a state-of-the-art system
trained with linguistic resources, with the latter outperforming our method in several
metrics despite our approach successfully producing intelligible and semi-natural
speech in the given conditions.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are employed to establish and refine the linear relaxations underlying this McCormick envelope framework. We've also analyzed the potential for local optimality solutions and validated our approach through simulations and real-world experiments on a walking robot.

We have developed a comprehensive method for determining the minimum number of measurements and operations required to transform one quantum state into another through probabilistic means. This method allows us to calculate the specific rate of successful state transformations and yields tighter bounds on the distance between quantum state sets than previously estimated. Furthermore, our results indicate that the rate of successful transformations approaches one as the dimension of the states increases. Additionally, our work has enabled the derivation of stricter limits on the rate of successful transformations in various specific scenarios and has implications for the study of quantum entanglement and non-locality.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the average angle of the coffee remained contained within a specific range, leading to steady periodic motion. However, vertical excitation led to amplification of the amplitude of the coffee, causing it to periodically swing at varying angles. When subjected to combined excitations, the average angle of the coffee increased and its motion became chaotic, characterized by extreme amplitude fluctuations. We observed that when the excitation frequency approximated half the pivot oscillation frequency, a resonant effect occurred, significantly amplifying the motion. The observed results are presented in the form of diagrams and maps that indicate stable, periodic, and chaotic regimes for the coffee in motion.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of decentralized machine learning over graph networks by developing an efficient new method, DR-DSGD, which incorporates a robustness criterion into the stabilization technique used by DSGD. By adapting the robustness criterion in relation to a reference distribution, which can be estimated using our empirical drift estimator, we derive a stable learning algorithm capable of reaching a statistically accurate state despite significant disturbances. We analytically prove that DR-DSGD achieves a precise solution for large-scale problems and demonstrate experimentally that it performs better than other competing decentralized learning algorithms.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, we derive a straightforward, numerically verifiable formula that accurately predicts the number of produced particles based on the initial energy state. This prediction not only aligns with experimental findings for smaller collisions, but also for larger ones, extending our previous successful model that was only applicable to lower energy collisions.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths. The results reveal a distinct two-stage process in jet formation, where initially, fast-moving jets develop, and then slowly, slower-moving jets emerge. During the initial phase, fast-moving jets dominate, their heads creating dense barriers that block the emergence of slower-moving jets. However, once the fast-moving jets weaken, a sudden increase in slower-moving jets occurs. This phenomenon is observed regardless of magnetic field strength, and the reason lies in the accumulation of material at the dense barriers, eventually leading to the breaking apart of the barriers and the emergence of slower-moving jets.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric, which measures system safety in the presence of an obstacle region by employing a continuous approximation of the nonlinear controller. A linearized model predictive control (LMPC) strategy is then developed based on the PSA and an optimized trajectory planning method, which leverages the specific structure of the balanced control law. Eventually, this methodology is applied to a quadrotor helicopter navigating through an obstacle course.

This study provides in-depth mathematical and computational examinations of a natural phenomenon where small celestial bodies are drawn to larger bodies like the Sun due to gravity, causing irregular orbits and potential fluctuations that can affect an object's long-term movement patterns in the Solar system, specifically identifying and analyzing areas with fluctuating patterns near the Sun's influence zone.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. It is noted that previously such models were developed without considering the technical intricacies of gauge invariance, which ensures accurate physical predictions. This short paper presents fundamental adjustments ensuring the consistency of these modified TB models, and it presents a unifying approach for both spin and charge based models, thereby standardizing the procedure for modeling coupled light-matter systems. Examples are provided to illustrate the impact of discontinuous electron density distributions and the relevance of gauge invariance even at low light amplitudes.

In a task-specific PBR (Perception, Tracking, Reconstruction, and Builing Recognition) pipeline, PCR (Category-level Object Recognition, Pose Recovery, and Shape Estimation) is a crucial component that provides a detailed 3D reconstruction of objects from various sources, such as 2D and 3D semantic keypoints. Our research focuses on the development of an optimal and robust PCR method, which utilizes a trained PCR network to estimate the 3D shape of objects from semantic keypoints in a direct manner. Our results show that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and we also provide detailed analyses and comparisons with other methods on the Category-level Object Recognition and Shape Estimation benchmark.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under the assumption that those subgroups aren't fundamentally different. The goal is to establish the optimal sample size for each subgroup before the trial begins. The approach uses historical control data to set a baseline and calculates probabilities of response based on a new treatment in each subgroup using a Bayesian approach. The probabilities of response in each subgroup are assumed to be the same as in the historical control group. A pre-defined effect size is then used to determine the required sample size for each subgroup. The approach works by simulating trial data for each subgroup and assessing whether the treatment induces a statistically significant improvement over the control group at an specified power level. If it doesn't show a significant improvement, the trial isn't considered successful. The process is repeated until we find the minimum sample size required for each subgroup that allows the treatment to show a significant improvement at a specified power level.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach's effectiveness in real-world applications is demonstrated through successful medical and mechanical anomaly detection experiments.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, then identify which elements in these groups generate twisted conjugacy classes.

To determine which collider is most suitable for confirming instability in the Standard Model, we create a collider twist on the Goldstone Friedberg-Tully model. This model features a new scalar boson, $\phi$, that can be produced at various colliders through the process $\ell^+\ell^-\gamma\phi$. We then generate spectra and rates for $\phi$ production at proton-proton, electron-positron, and lepton-proton colliders, using twostep MLLE EFT matching to MLLE. We consider instability energy windows of $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ to $1000\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and evaluate signal detection possibilities for $\phi$ production at $13\,\mathrm{TeV}$ LHC, $250\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $500\,\mathrm{GeV}$ ILC, $27\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $500\,\mathrm{GeV}$ CLIC, $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $250\,\mathrm{GeV}$ LHC, $90\,\mathrm{GeV}$ FWB, and future $e^-e^+$ colliders proposed in Beijing, Frankfurt, and Leipzig with $250\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $500\,\mathrm{GeV}$ center-of-mass energy. We observe that detecting the instability with high confidence will be most feasible at the $250\,\mathrm{GeV}$ ILC for nearly all considered energy windows, but the $

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction. Results from applying the technique accurately capture the rapid evolution of electronic and nuclear dynamics in both experiments. Furthermore, this approach is highly resilient to noisy data and provides a reliable estimate of the uncertainty in the calculated trajectory.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and a predominantly transverse light-front distribution.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces is determined by the conditions under which the inverse operations are permissible. Importantly, our findings have implications for the boundedness of Toeplitz operators within these spaces, resolving a long-standing issue for the $S_0^\omega$ space in particular.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual annotations presents a difficult task. We've discovered that generating synthetic data from annotated modalities through CycleGAN techniques introduces domain shift when using this data for segmentation. To overcome this challenge, we present the Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network (CSGAN), a model that simultaneously performs cycle-consistency training and supervise training using GANs. This approach allows our model to directly learn domain-invariant segmentation functions for unseen modalities. Experimental results show that CSGAN outperforms existing methods in performing UNet-like tasks for CT-to-MRI and MRI-to-CT transformation, with code available on GitHub.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features and outperforms state-of-the-art models, surpassing existing action
recognition and anticipation benchmarks.

AD Leo, a red dwarf star, is known for its frequent flare activity that can be studied to better understand stellar evolution and behavior. By analyzing UV images from the IUE satellite, researchers identified a major flare on April 12, 1985, that revealed intriguing details in the star's ultraviolet spectrum. Comparing observed data with models, it became clear that the optical properties of the flare's plasma needed to be reconsidered - specifically its absorption lines in the far-UV spectrum. Furthermore, the complexity of the optical behavior during this flare made it challenging to model its spectrum using a single uniform plasma. Instead, researchers proposed a two-component model consisting of a hot plasma and a cooler region overlying it. As a result of this new approach, the two-component model was found to effectively align observed and predicted spectra across a wide range of wavelengths, resolving discrepancies in the optical behavior during this flare.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is finite-dimensional. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and discuss the general applicability of these findings to the specific case of nearly K3 surfaces.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, commencing at a vertex representing a p multiple.
