This graphical representation provides insight, revealing that existing research on largest p-core p'-partitions is a subset of this graph's stationary distribution computations. Building on this connection, the paper develops two efficient algorithms for calculating largest p-core p'-partitions. While one algorithm runs in p-time, optimized for smaller p values, the second algorithm has a linear scale of p but excels for larger p values. Additionally, the paper's methods allow for generalizing these findings to largest p-core (p+s)-partitions, expanding the scope of p-core partition research.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have proven vulnerable to manipulations like adversarial attacks and natural image conversions. Current defense methods are often either universally applicable or focused on specific attack types and do not translate to other situations. Researchers have found that using geometric invariants can effectively protect against various types of attacks, but their previously proposed methods require complicated decoding processes and have not been tested against the most sophisticated attacks on 3D data. To address these limitations, this study introduces an innovative technique called TPC, which uses a transformation-specific smoothing method for 3D point clouds. TPC can effectively defend against a broad range of attacks, has a lightweight design, and efficiently removes adversarial perturbations without significantly altering the point cloud's shape and position. Experimental results show that TPC outperforms other defense methods, is more versatile than previously proposed techniques, and can be adapted for other 3D models with minor modifications.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we identify a sweet spot for minimum interference where the radar system operates efficiently. We observe that CSMA performs better than ALOHA but introduce new parameters to enhance ALOHA's performance, now on par with CSMA under certain conditions. We apply these medium access protocols in various radar applications.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference pattern resulting from entangled photons interacting with a beam splitter and two quantum absorbers. Based on this concept, the study presents a theoretical model for detecting non-linear optical effects within a single crystal utilizing a quantum entanglement-sensitive method. By examining the spectral properties of photons, the researchers were able to clearly identify a notable signature of entangled two-photon absorption, demonstrating the efficacy of this innovative approach.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share key similarities with the T^2-action on CP(V) being free and the T-action commuting with T^2. As a result, CP(V) serves as a locus for the theory to be freely T-doubly extended. This freedom allows us to show that the T-equivariant cohomology of CP(V) is isomorphic to the T-doubly extended cohomology of the T-representation V. This is accomplished by reducing to this situation the findings of Bar22 and combining them with results from Gre05.

Knowledge graph completion relies on generating likely relationships between entities based on existing knowledge. This study focuses on filling in missing links between entities over time. Current approaches have overlooked the potential information contained in time stamps and the connections between entities that appear together at the same time point. Specifically, this work addresses entity relationship predictions by taking a multi-task learning approach that considers (1) low-rank representations for each knowledge graph attribute to capture shared patterns across time, (3) using a model-agnostic vector set that represents the characteristics of each knowledge graph attribute independently of any specific model. This approach is combined with the development of a dataset, KGBIO-T, which includes biomedical entities along with their associated temporal context. The efficacy of this method is evaluated using KGBIO-T and another existing dataset, WB.

In first-person shooter games, players frequently overlook ground sound effects as a source of information, focusing mainly on visual cues. This research aims to highlight the importance of ground sound through an artificial intelligence opponent that leverages it to gain an advantage. A sound detection system capable of identifying relevant sounds, orienting the source, and estimating distance has been developed. A test of this system's effectiveness involved competitive matches between human players and the created AI opponent, demonstrating that the AI gained a significant advantage when ground sound was utilized.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as $\pi^-$ and $\pi^+$. This species of correlations, derived from $\pi$-mutations of Wigner's original scenario, necessitates at least one continuous variable in the measurement space to manifest the all-versus-nothing phenomenon, thereby indicating its local impossibility. Construction of a specific $\pi^+$ correlation in the context of four qubit systems provides insight into its origins and potential applications. Furthermore, this correlation serves as a resource for violating Bell inequalities, with its non-inequality-based all-versus-nothing proof offering valuable insights into this relationship.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems fall under this category, such as the zero modes in Kitaev materials and the zero modes supported by topological superconductors, characterized by non-zero MO symmetry protections despite being located at flat bands.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm structure, exhibits an indirect bandgap. However, upon applying hydrostatic pressure of up to 100 GPa, the system transforms into the CsB$_4$ structure with a semiconductor to metal transition, along with an unexpected absence of superconductivity. The analysis suggests weak electron-phonon coupling and an extremely small phase-space fraction in the Brillouin zone where Fermi surface states reside, contributing to the non-superconducting nature. Furthermore, the presence of a flat band in the ideal Cmmm state hinders multiband superconductivity, whereas the large compression introduced by high pressure replaces this band with a local minimum, preventing a pairing mechanism essential for superconductivity.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here extend the concept of a lattice distribution, where each element in a set of n items is uniquely assigned to a set of k items, to the case where assignments are not unique. Additionally, a specific formula is provided for the number of ways to divide n items into k parts, where the division is done in a random order. The concept of "flattened partitions" is introduced, which involves dividing n items into k parts where some parts can have repeated items. A specific formula is given for the number of ways to divide n items into k parts, where the division is done in a random order.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this regard, prompting us to propose an advanced method utilizing model checking technology. By representing system states with focus on control flow and output patterns rather than low-level signal dynamics, we can effectively tackle this verification challenge. To demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach, we conduct in-depth case studies on a fail-operational automotive driving system, successfully verifying its compliance with industry standards in critical failure scenarios.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state transition matrix and an influence matrix that quantifies the predictive value of each node for its peers. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering synthetic data sets of various shapes and sizes, as well as real-world data sets comprising chaotic attractors and mixed patterns.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, one which incorporates both infinites and denominations with an order, as well as the differential calculus's essential features.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that we have created, making predictions about how the analysis will go. These expectations include the accuracy of the best fit parameters, the likelihood contours, the bias of the best fit parameters, and the impact on the results of foreground subtraction methods. Our expectations are that the best fit parameters will be accurate to a few percent, the likelihood contours will be elongated because of foregrounds, biases will be smallest at certain redshifts because of a part of the spectrum that is less affected by foregrounds, and that the shape of the HI intensity mapping power spectrum will be best constrained at a certain wavenumber because of a sweet spot in where the signal and foregrounds contribute compared to each other.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition like $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ must hold for some injection $\phi$ of $i$ into the natural numbers, then the sequence ${e_i}$ can only be linearly independent if the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite.

One key factor driving the rapid growth of the digital environment is our ever-increasing reliance on personalization. Various recommender systems have been developed to tackle this issue, primarily focusing on addressing the inherent data scarcity issue encountered during system implementation and initial user data collection. Our study aims to address this problem by integrating two complementary methods - document-based and behavior-based - to enhance the accuracy and user satisfaction of the recommender system. Our approach, which incorporates an explicit agreement algorithm into the rating-based and click-through data-based collaborative filtering method, yields superior performance. When compared to other state-of-the-art recommender systems, our integrated approach consistently outperforms them in achieving improved precision and recall ratios.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ matrices with var$(a_{ij})\le 1$ exhibit several forms of noncommutativity. The asymptotic behavior of $M_N(a)$ in noncommutative probability space, particularly for $M_N(a)$ with $a<1$, reveals an interesting connection - it characterizes the forms of noncommutativity for all unitarily invariant matrices. We discover that $M_N(a)$ also possesses an equivalent representation in terms of independent complex Toeplitz matrices or as a specific type of Wigner matrix. This finding is further extended to obtain an estimate of asymptotic noncommutativity for general $M_N(a)$.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Isoscalar scalar mesons, $f_0(980)$ and $f_0(1500)$,
undergo a thorough study in terms of their production and mixing processes.
Evidence suggests that $f_0(980)$ contains a significant $K^*0 \bar K^0$ component
with little $J/\psi \pi^0$ content, and $f_0(980)$'s couplings to $J/\psi \pi^0
\eta$ are calculated by utilizing unitary up to the $f_0(980)(a_0(980))\pi^0$
channel. Additionally, $f_0(1500)$ and $f_0(1370)$ are considered for
reference. Our study provides branching ratios for $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$
and suggests an upper limit for $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a pupil tracker, a beam tracker, a finder, and a re-injection system. Employing a $2 \times 2$ array of lenses and filters alongside a $4 \times 4$ electronic detector, the camera offers versatile optical configurations that facilitate the re-direction of beam sums and pupil images. Furthermore, it enables the simultaneous detection of all four beams in conjunction with pupil tracking, contributing to an enhanced understanding of GRAVITY's performance. The camera has undergone thorough characterization, which is discussed in this paper.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class. This distinction is the first documented case where a problem's hardness is distinguished based on a graph's geometric property.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because the underlying computations are carried out using noisy values obtained from measurements of the polynomial linear system. A key concept in this study is the quality of a polynomial, which is defined as the minimum degree of polynomials with zero interpolation values. This research provides an alternative solution to the problem posed in 2019 by J. Berlekamp, M. Kumar, and S. Basu, and extends the approach to systems with errors, while also proposing an early termination technique that dynamically stops computations when sufficient information has already been obtained. Unlike existing solutions that require the same amount of computations as the best known bounds, this research demonstrates that the same quality of solution can be achieved with significantly fewer computations, specifically with a reduction to linear complexity.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

In the context of distributed systems, network size estimation is a crucial issue 
when creating random samples for statistical analysis or distributed algorithms. 
Present methods for large networks are either inefficient or unreliable in the presence 
of malicious activity. This study provides accurate and reliable algorithms for 
estimating a large network's size when affected by a limited number of malicious nodes.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging this method, we demonstrate the generation of initial data for black hole spacetimes in various states, including rotation and higher dimensional variants.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and analyzing the data, the experiment's researchers gained valuable insights into the various parameters of the instruments, including dark current and photopeak values. This knowledge enabled the researchers to further develop and refine the evaluation criteria for the experiment's selection process. As a result, the knowledge gained and the developed protocols can be applied to other large-scale scintillator-based detectors, such as the Hyper-Kamiokande project, for the evaluation and improvement of 20-inch PMTs.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results, but it faces challenges like parameter instability that complicates model training and diminishes performance. To address these issues, this paper proposes an LSTF framework built around an improved adaptive graph convolutional network structure, incorporating features like parameter adaptability, data dimensionality awareness, and long-term information incorporation through knowledge augmentation. The proposed framework is rigorously tested on real-world datasets, including energy consumption and air quality datasets, and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, demonstrating its practical value in practical multidimensional time series prediction scenarios.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address these concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range. A network of sensors, rather than just a single sensor, can enhance sensitivity by measuring the cross-correlations between signals, rather than just their amplitude.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A uniqueness criterion based on the number of low-frequency Fourier components has been established for BPC, which matches the results obtained from the restricted isometry property (RIP) for the discrete case. Furthermore, a convex relaxation approach for recovering two-dimensional Radon measures through BPC has been developed and proven to be unique in specific scenarios.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. The P4 syntax is vast and complex, making it challenging for programmers to translate P4 programs into hardware-compatible code. Although commercial tools can simplify this process, they often tie developers to specific hardware platforms, restrict program modification, and compromise performance. To address these issues, we have developed an open-source P416 compiler that targets the V1Model architecture. Our compiler can translate P4 programs into multiple hardware platforms, optimize table sizes, and adapt programs to different syntax versions. Additionally, it includes tools for generating flow tables, testing P4 programs, and performing hardware simulations.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocities or velocities multiplied by a scalar function. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that use the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two post-processing methods that aim to enhance the accuracy of transporting scalar functions across computational domains. One method builds upon a previously established post-processing technique for the transport equation, while the other involves using an adaptive grid strategy based on the discrete transport error. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods through a range of numerical experiments, specifically by solving flow problems in complex domains and examining both steady and unsteady scenarios.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study presents the first unified framework that integrates fairness assessment and differential privacy within Federated Learning. By drawing on Bregman divergences, this method offers a versatile framework that can be applied to numerous loss functions and optimizers, maintaining both computational efficiency and scalability comparable to state-of-the-art techniques. The proposed framework is then used to tackle regression, classification, and counterfactual fairness challenges.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, B_c^+. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-Critic-Training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries exhibit self-intersections, whereas a small amount of dissipation causes the emergence of Wada basins, increased topological entropy, and an expansion of the scattering phase regime. This study employs Wada order and detects Wada patterns through a quantitative measure called the Wada index, which has been applied to various Hamiltonian systems, including a kicked rotor model. The results show that the extent of Wada features is highly sensitive to the level of dissipation, and this three-dimensional system offers an ideal model for experimenting with quantum delocalization in systems that exhibit Wada basins.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments such as the NUMAS experiment. For example, we can investigate the muon decay atom experiment's sensitivity to this scalar's interaction within a different window. Lastly, we examine the potential detection of these scalar particles by the PTOLEMY experiment at an underground facility or the COHERENT experiment using a reactor-based setup within a particular window.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance and a competitive edge over other state-of-the-art methods.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The research additionally examines the validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture in charged black holes following a different scattering process.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, particularly within dense gas installations. SF's initial identification, characterized by bright infrared radiation, will be discussed in detail, along with the role of magnetic fields, which cannot be seen directly. The process of SF is a complex and highly dynamic phenomenon, influenced by a variety of physical factors, ultimately giving rise to the formation of solar-type stars and, intriguingly, brown dwarfs. In recent years, significant breakthroughs have been achieved in understanding SF, primarily by combining observational data from radio to mm and submm wavelengths, along with analytical models and sophisticated computational tools. These advancements have not only expanded our knowledge but also exposed some longstanding enigmas, which will be highlighted in this article.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex fluid interactions and develop new solutions for a related conservation equation, focusing on situations where solutions may not be single-valued or may not exist at all. This involves considering a distension function that may take on non-zero values. We introduce a new definition for solutions and establish that in the absence of discontinuities, this solution mirrors the classical solution. Furthermore, by incorporating a small parameter in the equation, we demonstrate the existence of weak measure-valued solutions for the original conservation law. This approach is then illustrated with examples in one and two dimensions, and we discuss the challenges involved in extending these methods to more complex scenarios.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it by allowing high accuracy classifications at rapid speeds. However, AI-driven classifiers often require substantial amounts of data and advanced computing power to function effectively, hindering their application on low-power devices such as microcontrollers. To address this limitation, we have developed NBcoded, a novel classifier system that leverages Naive Bayes and Encoder models to provide accurate classifications for network attack datasets. The system's compact size and low computational complexity enable it to operate seamlessly on tiny microcontrollers, making it an ideal solution for resource-constrained IoT devices.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it has a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap is given by n^p. We also discuss some classifications of finitely presented torsion-free solvable groups with growth functions n and n^2 respectively.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with other characteristics extracted from moving entities, a classification system can effectively classify biolocomotion. To further enhance the proposed approach, additional criteria such as the presence of tails and specific patterns in movement are introduced. Ultimately, a decision tree classifier is used to determine whether a detected moving entity is biolocomoting or not. The method was tested using a dataset of approximately 20,000 frames, collected from the wild in the Amazon rainforest, featuring a wide range of biological species, including fish, frogs, insects, and birds. The proposed approach achieved a high level of accuracy in detecting biolocomotion, with results indicating its potential applicability in ecology, wildlife monitoring, management of natural resources, agricultural management, searchengines for wildlife monitoring, medical procedures, film industry, advertising industry, photography, surveyor tools

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have successfully optimized problem-solving in numerous domains, yet the underlying physical principles that govern these environments remain unlearned. In most cases, physical laws are discovered through intuitive reasoning and not from data analysis. This study investigates whether AI algorithms can automatically extract universal physical laws from large datasets without prior knowledge of the laws. We find that large neural networks can identify regular patterns in complex data and uncover underlying physical relationships but only when the data is consistent and complete. When data is inconsistent or incomplete, these networks either fail to make predictions or provide inaccurate results. We discuss the implications of these findings and propose future research directions to develop intelligent systems that can autonomously extract physical principles from real-world data.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, and other scenarios. The results are presented in tables showing the 95% confidence level limits on the production cross-sections for these hypothetical particles and are also depicted as mass-versus-lifetime contours in figures for comparison with theoretical predictions.

We improve the photon collection efficiency in ridge waveguide-based sources from 60% to near-unity levels (over 99%) by using a proprietary ridge waveguide material. This improved efficiency enhances single-photon source performance by increasing the probability of emitting a single photon. We verify the high efficiency of the source through measurement of the correlated photon pairs' joint quantum state, and document the improved properties of the source, including the single-photon purity, conditional purity, and single-photon probability. This optimized system has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of various quantum communication applications and technologies.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction where the boson peak and transition temperature are equivalent.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. A numerical approach called 
difference equations helps in such difficult cases, although evaluating these 
equations at different physical scenarios is challenging. A new publication 
investigates the application of difference equations to multi-loop, multi-scale 
Feynman integrals using an innovative approach called the C++ library MATAIL. 
This library allows users to specify physical scenarios through real-world 
parameters, rather than the complex mathematical concepts of loop integrals. 
The library's evaluation is then compared with traditional analytical solutions 
using modern mathematical techniques. The results show that difference equations 
can accurately compute even the most complex single-particle behavior and 
production processes in particle physics, also providing a built-in error 
evaluation. The library MATAIL is available for download at the repository 
10.24415/v2e1.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side spiral arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distributions. Based on these findings, it's suggested that these arms are relatively old, having formed about 70 million years ago, and are dynamically linked. This research also provides constraints on the Milky Way's rotation curve, which are consistent with those from other methods, and further confirms that the arms are primarily composed of molecular gas.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, ultimately enhancing solution diversity.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical structures. A fundamental condition in this context is that each agent's preferences are consistent across rankings. A novel variant of this problem, with the three-dimensional version of additively separable preferences, is explored in this paper. A polynomial-time algorithm is proposed to find stable and efficient matchings in this scenario. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that while the problem of finding the most stable matching has connections to combinatorial optimization, it actually belongs to the class of NP-complete problems.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that a significant increase in
carriable valley degeneracy occurs. The introduction of a constant charge density
also leads to a significant increase, with all charges having the same valley index.
Our findings indicate that the valley Hall effect can arise due to a symmetric and
asymmetric electron-phonon interaction, and that a finite magnetic field can
eliminate the valley dependence in some electron-phonon coupling constants.
Additionally, our research demonstrates that valley separation at twisted
interfaces is possible even without magnetic field effects, and that the valley
Hall effect can occur at these interfaces due to a lack of valley degeneracy.
Furthermore, our findings indicate that multi-valley electronics based on electron-
phonon interaction can be used to generate complex magnetic field patterns.
Finally, our research suggests that the use of superlattices based on electron-phonon
interaction could enable the creation of quantum Hall states at zero magnetic
field.

In the framework of Gromov-Hausdorff distance, we define and study "clouds," which are complete subsets of compact subsets of geometric metric spaces. We demonstrate that every compact subset itself constitutes a cloud. The primary objectives of this paper involve establishing the completeness of clouds, as well as identifying central subsets within these clouds. Our research provides a fundamental completeness theorem for the original Gromov-Hausdorff distance, offering an alternative method for evaluating distance between individual points and clouds. We also introduce a new distance metric for central subsets of geometric metric spaces, which met with successful outcomes in functional analysis applications.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angular range has been successfully created and tested. The antenna features a simple microstrip matching circuit and integrates a microstrip feedback loop, which contributes to its expanded angular coverage. Built with affordable and low-loss microstrip technology, this antenna design is ideal for integration in microstrip circuits. The designed antenna operates within an expanded bandwidth of 7.3 GHz, covering the frequency range from 26.2 GHz to 33.5 GHz. Furthermore, it exhibits a wide horizontal beamwidth and a slightly narrower vertical beamwidth, making it suitable for high-gain applications such as 5G, wireless communication, and biomedical devices operating at mm-waves.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by exploiting entangled quantum states to estimate parameters such as phase. This paper proposes a method for measuring phase using a quantum jump-based approach in a two-cavity network. The method assembles an entangled state across cavities by exchanging photons, allowing for the determination of phase with exceptional resolution. The proposed system includes two cavities connected by an optical fiber cavity, with input from a laser that induces entanglement through a series of controlled interactions. The entanglement is then destroyed as the laser re-enters the cavities, creating a sequence of distinct emission events known as "quantum jumps". The interference pattern resulting from these jumps provides precise information about the phase with high resolution. The approach has the potential to be the most efficient method yet for this type of measurement and could be implemented with currently available technology.

Researchers have measured correlations between direct photons and hadrons in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at 200 GeV. They analyzed data from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, focusing on direct photons created in the early stages of collisions. By examining these correlations, they found evidence of jet suppression in Au+Au collisions, but not in d+Au collisions, suggesting that jet suppression occurs primarily when a high-energy parton interacts with the dense medium. Moreover, the magnitude of jet suppression appears to depend on the angle between the parton's direction and the photon's direction.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without quantum error-correction, by utilizing near-analog quantum states that are only slightly distorted to meet the requirements of being representable by classical-logic-compatible quantum states. We explore a quantum simulation of fermionic systems using this hybrid approach and find that digital-analog states remain suitable for the simulation of fermionic systems, even when subjected to distortion. We also examine near-analog states that are close to fermionic systems but can't be distorted, and find that they enable successful fermionic simulation with high success probabilities. We discuss the implications of these findings on quantum chemistry and solid-state physics simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can impede training and impair performance. This study presents an alternative approach, allowing for the incorporation of rich features into the model without the need for penalty terms, thereby avoiding performance degradation. The proposed rich features are generated by an autoencoder that is trained separately, resulting in encoded representations that capture essential characteristics of the data and can be easily adapted for use in downstream tasks. The method has been rigorously evaluated on multiple benchmarks, yielding superior performance compared to previous methods.

Achieving rapid and precise control of tissue shape at the cellular level holds significant promise for the fields of cell biology and bio-photonics. A novel multi-pointed iterative approach to controlling tissue morphology is described, utilizing a lightweight liquid-crystal spatial light modulator to simultaneously form multiple intricate patterns within a single three-dimensional volume. By applying this method, we successfully created various complex patterns in a tissue-like medium, including a detailed replica of the Roman numeral 'III'. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using this light-control technique to control tissue morphology with resolutions in the range of tens of micrometers.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, implications, and approaches. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that for efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and electrical properties of the sensors. Two CLICTD sensors were tested, one built on a high-resistivity substrate with a thick epitaxial layer and high collector concentration, and another built on a low-resistivity implant layer. The results show that the active sensor depth is approximately 30 μm, while the corresponding reduced sensitive volume is around 15 μm. This study aids in optimizing design parameters for enhanced sensitive volumes in future CLICTD modules.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with current systems unable to effectively eliminate the interference caused by atmospheric speckles. These speckles can still distort ground-based telescope images, even if adaptive optics have been implemented, due to their rapid movement and small scale. Consequently, there is a need for a more efficient and real-time speckle removal technology that can be easily integrated into existing systems. Specifically, it should be capable of processing high frame rates, handling large speckle fields, and working with large telescopes under poor atmospheric conditions. Our testbed at the Santa cruz facility represents such an innovative solution, with our system successfully reducing spekele power by over ten times across a 39 x 39 pixel area, with an average image scale equivalent to 180 x 180 micrometers. Our system achieves this through a unique fast atmospheric self-coherent camera technique that uses a small telescope to focus a narrow field of view, modulate the wavefront, and then direct the remaining energy back to the original entrance aperture. With our system, we recorded a 26.7 Hz video sequence for 0.53 seconds under severe atmospheric conditions, with our wavefront control algorithm successfully controlling the spekele power throughout the entire duration. Our system has demonstrated its potential

This study presents a novel exogenous short-rate model, which we call the deterministic-shift Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model. We've modified the original CIR model by introducing a special type of jump for immediate purposes. The motivation behind our approach lies in the Euromarket data's negative observations. We've selected numerical strategies for solving the yield curve calibration problem that are both easy to understand and highly effective. We've also analyzed various dynamic hedging exercises, including both static and interactive scenarios. Our analysis reveals that the reliability of hedges is directly affected by the interest rate's volatility. We've supported our findings with explicit numerical results.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past and planned experiments such as SHiP, for neutrino masses up to approximately 350 MeV. We visualize these results through exclusion plots created using established benchmarks.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively account for within-study correlations, however this approach may produce biased results when including trials that share study participants as if they were independent entities.  In order to address this issue, a new cluster-robust meta-regression approach called the jackknife estimate has been developed.  The jackknife estimate modifies the standard cluster-robust variance estimator by accounting for within-study correlations as well as the number of shared study participants, thereby providing an unbiased estimate of the test statistic's distribution.  The proposed approach was implemented in the meta R package meta4eR and evaluated using simulations and three actual research studies.  Additionally, a method for estimating the variance of the test statistic's distribution has been proposed and implemented.  This method involves using the jackknife estimate to smooth out extreme outliers that may skew the estimate of the test statistic's distribution.  The proposed approach was found to be superior to existing methods in terms of accuracy and performance.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, but this approach is not physically accurate and can lead to incorrect predictions of particle collision rates and distributions. Our proposed method directly uses the physical collision time associated with each particle collision event, allowing for significantly larger time steps. To achieve this, we integrated the Molecular Dynamics method for resolving particle collisions into a computational fluid dynamics framework. This integration involved developing new techniques to handle particles moving rapidly into the vicinity of an particle collision event and to ensure numerical stability. Our results show that this new method performs well for a wide range of conditions, including high particle concentrations and a broad spectrum of particle size ratios.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in different contexts. Specifically, the models rely on different descriptions of the interaction between partons and the nucleons that make up the nucleus, according to color dipole framework, which considers the re-scattering of partons as they travel through the nucleus. Although transverse momentum broadening is generally observed across all models, notable discrepancies arise when comparing this effect for different parton species, such as charged particles, where experimental data from the LHC suggest a potential contradiction to certain theoretical predictions.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal re-execution costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a remarkably low overhead, with the majority of these experiments resulting in zero overhead. Even in cases where some re-execution of computations is necessary to correct errors, the overhead is still remarkably low, at less than 6 percent, thus making this approach an attractive solution for ensuring fault-tolerant HPC applications.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts hierarchical structures from large networks, even at a massive data scale, and is specifically designed for web-based applications.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we studied the distribution of perihelion distances and orbital periods. Our results show that the perihelion distribution follows a power-law pattern, specifically a stretched exponential function, and the perihelion values and orbital periods exhibit significant scatter. Moreover, we discovered that the perihelion values often display long-term memory effects. By contrast, the theoretical model accurately predicts the exponential decay of escape velocity orbits but overestimates the survival times for colliding orbits. Nevertheless, our research reveals that the statistical flux approach provides a reliable prediction of the real system's trends, including the scaling of escape velocities and the shape of colliding orbit decay curves.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, and that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons is comparable to that of $\psi$(2S) mesons. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons is similar to suppression found in studies of U and Pb collisions at lower energies, but that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than in those studies. The study found that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, and that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons is comparable to suppression found in studies of both prompt and non-prompt mesons.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant polarization level of $9.1\pm2.8$ percent at 5-9 keV in observations of Cassiopeia A using the IXPE telescope. By analyzing the polarization angle, we found that it matches the direction of diffuse X-ray emission within the supernova remnant, suggesting an interplay of polarization from both synchrotron radiation and isotropic inverse Compton radiation. By examining the polarization map, we observed variability across the remnant, leading to a conclusion that the synchrotron radiation dominates in the northwestern shell, whereas the isotropic inverse Compton radiation dominates in the southern blob. Furthermore, we estimated a lower limit on magnetic field strength of approximately $100$ Gauss in the northwestern shell. Our findings provide new insights into the overall polarization pattern in Cassiopeia A, offering a better understanding of its synchrotron and isotropic inverse Compton radiation components.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars with and without quark matter, have been extensively studied. At such densities, the dense matter may comprise of nucleons, strange hadrons, and quarks. In this research, a table top density separator is utilized to separate a mixture of dense matter components. By simulating the dense matter formation process using magnetic fields, initial conditions leading to distinct component separations are established. With the assumption that magnetic fields cause components with different charges to separate, a model of dense matter comprising of nucleons, strange hadrons, and quarks is constructed, and the resulting sound velocity calculations are presented. In this model, the dense matter consists of three distinct components: free quarks at the highest densities, quark-dense hadron mixture at intermediate densities, and a mixture of nucleons and strange hadrons at the lowest densities. The sound velocity in such a model is found to be extremely high at densities around 5-6 times nuclear saturation density, which could lead to the phenomenon of the causal ultrahigh frequency oscillations in the star's crust. In this model, the dense matter comprising of nucleons, strange hadrons, and quarks, the sound velocity, and the resulting properties of the compact stars are presented in detail.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining how their phase space structure changes with different levels of squeezing and displacement across multiple frequency ranges. Our analysis reveals that in the high-frequency regime, states with increased coherence but reduced phonon content can be considered "compass states", offering a middle ground between traditional squeezed vacuum states, which offer efficient cooling, and displaced squeezed states, which serve as a platform for ground-state cooling laser cooling techniques.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently captures the dynamics of multi-component flows with distinct interfaces, we successfully simplify the representation of a periodic liquid jet. This involves propagating a gradient through the structure and simultaneously managing the appearance and disappearance of interfaces, ultimately allowing the recovery of the original geometry from the skeletal information.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, performance, and efficiency. The findings from this study align with experimental data, as reported in the referenced papers.

Our research reveals a connection between the occurrence of U-type warping in galaxies and the phenomenon of tidal disruption and heating, particularly evident in "jellyfish" galaxies resulting from group or cluster interactions. By conducting a detailed morphological analysis of a dataset of ~185,000 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 13, we identified a significant relationship between U-type warping and galaxies experiencing tidal forces. These findings are supported by simulations, which demonstrate that U-type warping is predominantly caused by the group/cluster center's gravitational pull and the transmission of waves throughout the galaxy disk. Additionally, our research found that galaxies undergoing tidal disruption and heating are more likely to display U-type warping than those experiencing other types of distortions.

This research presents a corrected version of the established Liouville theorem for scalar curvature shrinkers with constant scalar curvature. The initial proof contained an error, particularly in the estimation of the Laplacian operator's norm, which has been resolved and refined in this revised version. Additionally, the corrected theorem's consequences include an improved version of Chen's maximum principle and an enhanced version of Cai and Cao's theorem regarding the uniform convergence of a specific equation's solutions.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry are preserved in these crystals, the predicted phonons exhibit exceptional softness at the Brillouin zone center. Notably, this property can differentiate between materials consisting of only potassium and those composed of its lighter counterparts, rubidium and cesium. This discovery presents an opportunity to apply pressure to these materials, potentially inducing a phase transition and creating a state with broken time reversal symmetry.
